title: The Trust Game
text:
Economic theory long assumed that strangers who would never meet again had no reason to trust each other. In 1995 Joyce Berg, John Dickhaut and Kevin McCabe of the University of Minnesota designed a game to see what real people do.

Students were split into two rooms and paired anonymously, so no one ever learned who their partner was, and even the experimenters could not link choices to individuals. Each person in the first room received 10 dollars. They could keep it all or send any part of it to their partner in the other room. Whatever they sent was tripled on the way. The partner then decided how much, if any, of the tripled amount to send back.

A purely selfish partner would return nothing, and a sender who expected that would send nothing. That is not what happened. Nearly all senders sent some money, on average about half of their 10 dollars. Many receivers returned money too, some more than had been sent, though others kept everything. On average, senders got back about as much as they had sent, or slightly less. The game, now known as the trust game or investment game, became a standard tool for studying trust and reciprocity around the world.
lesson: Most people are willing to extend some trust to strangers, and many repay it. Trusting first is a risk, but it is often the only way to start something good.
people: Joyce Berg, John Dickhaut, Kevin McCabe
source: Berg, J., Dickhaut, J., and McCabe, K. (1995). Trust, reciprocity, and social history. Games and Economic Behavior, 10(1), 122-142.
